lessons.title: Why analytics needs its own model
lessons.why: "Let's have the report just read the same database as the app" — a proposal that comes up on every other project. It saves a day at the start and costs months later. Being able to explain why this isn't done comes up before you even start building the model itself.
lessons.form:
A source (OLTP) answers "what's happening with this order right now" and is optimized for writes: data is spread across dozens of narrow tables, so one change touches one row.

A reporting model (OLAP) answers "what happened across all orders over two years" and is optimized for reads: wide fact tables with small lookup tables next to them.
lessons.example:
The requester's question: "revenue by category for the quarter."

In a reporting model that's one fact table and one product lookup: sum revenue, break it down by category. Two objects, one relationship.
lessons.reads: The report reads exactly the data it needs, without getting in the way of checkout — the model refreshes at night and lives apart from the production database.
lessons.wrong: The same question, as a query straight against the production database: join orders, order_lines, products, product_categories, category_tree, and sum by the top level of the tree.
lessons.wrongWhy: It will work — right up to the day fifty people open the report at once and a heavy query collides with the same database that's handling checkout. A second bill arrives later: the source's structure changes for the app's needs, not the report's, and one day a renamed column silently breaks the reporting.
lessons.selfCheck: Ask yourself: does this query compete for resources with whatever is making money right now? If yes, there needs to be a layer between it and the source.

lessons.title: Fact grain
lessons.why: The first question for any fact table is "what does one row mean." Without an answer, you can't sum correctly or compare honestly: two tables at different levels of detail in one report give numbers that are each correct on their own and meaningless side by side.
lessons.form:
Grain is written as a list joined by a multiplication sign — one dimension per factor:

  week × outlet × SKU

If that combination occurs exactly once in the table, the grain has been named correctly.
lessons.example: fact_sellout: one row is the sales of one SKU at one outlet for one week. There are 118,449 rows, and exactly that many distinct "week × outlet × SKU" combinations.
lessons.reads: The match between row count and combination count is the proof: the key isn't duplicated, so the grain is described exactly, not approximately.
lessons.wrong: "One row of fact_sellout is one purchase."
lessons.wrongWhy: The phrasing sounds natural and is almost always wrong: a register rings up dozens of receipts a week, while the table has one row per SKU for that week. It's already an aggregate, not an event. The mistake surfaces on "how many purchases were there" — this table has no answer to that at all, and people usually bring the row count instead of an answer.
lessons.selfCheck: Check it by counting: the row count and the count of distinct combinations of the key dimensions should match. If they don't, the grain is actually finer than you thought.

lessons.title: Star and snowflake
lessons.why: An extract arrives as one wide table, with product name, brand, category, city and region sitting right next to sales. The temptation to leave it as is is real — it works, doesn't it. The star schema is why it gets split into a fact table and lookups anyway.
lessons.form:
A fact is what gets measured and accumulated: units, revenue. A dimension is what you slice it by: product, outlet, date, promo.

  fact in the center, dimensions around it — a star
  a dimension split further — a snowflake
lessons.example: fact_sellout (118,449 rows) plus dim_product (47), dim_customer (144), dim_promo (89), dim_date. The "category" attribute sits as a column inside dim_product — five categories across forty-seven products.
lessons.reads: The product name is stored 47 times — once per product — not 118,449 times, once per sales row. Editing the name happens in one place and shows up in every report immediately.
lessons.wrong: Keep one flat table of 118,449 rows, where product_name, brand, category, city and region_name sit as columns next to revenue.
lessons.wrongWhy: The most expensive thing here isn't disk space — it's consistency. Rename a product and the edit has to be carried into every row it appeared in, and any row you miss turns into a stray extra category in the filter. And the reverse case: a product that never sold this year simply doesn't exist in a table like this, so a "sales by all SKUs" report has no row for it with a zero.
lessons.selfCheck: Ask of every column in the fact table: is it measured, or does it describe? If it describes, it belongs in a lookup table, where it's stored once.

lessons.title: Relationships and cardinality
lessons.why: A relationship in a model isn't the same thing as a JOIN in a query. A JOIN combines rows; a relationship sets the direction a filter will travel along it. A report where a slicer doesn't affect half the measures is almost always explained by exactly this.
lessons.form:
A relationship has two properties, and they must not be confused:

  cardinality — how many rows on each side correspond to one row on the other (one-to-many, many-to-many)
  filter direction — lookup to fact by default, not the reverse
lessons.example: dim_product (47 rows, product_id unique) → fact_sellout (118,449 rows): one-to-many. Pick brand «Чистовъ» in a slicer — the filter travels from lookup to fact, and the revenue sum computes across that brand's five products.
lessons.reads: The "one" side filters the "many" side: the lookup sets which fact rows take part in the calculation.
lessons.wrong: Expecting a slicer on promo in dim_promo to filter dim_product the same way — "show the products that took part in the promo."
lessons.wrongWhy: The filter will reach from dim_promo into fact_sellout, and stop there: it doesn't flow back into dim_product by default — that's the "many"-to-"one" direction. The product list stays at its full 47, and that isn't a bug, it's the default behaviour — turning the reverse direction on takes a deliberate choice, and it has a cost.
lessons.selfCheck: Before you get surprised by a number, trace the filter's path with your finger from the slicer to the table where the measure computes. Did it get there, and did it change direction along the way?

lessons.title: Two paths to the same table
lessons.why: The most expensive modeling mistake looks harmless: another relationship got added because "it's more convenient to filter this way." After that, the report either refuses to compute, or — worse — computes and returns a number several times bigger than the real one.
lessons.form: There should be exactly one path from a fact table to a lookup. If there are two, the model doesn't pick the better one — it either bans the second relationship (leaves it inactive), or, if the join is made directly in a query, multiplies rows across every match.
lessons.example: fact_sellout links to dim_promo by promo_id — that's the correct path: a sales row either has a promo or it doesn't. The table's total revenue is ₽126,911,191, and along this path it stays that way.
lessons.reads: One path, one value. Every sales row corresponds to exactly one promo, or none.
lessons.wrong: Add a second path: fact_sellout → dim_product by product_id, then dim_product → dim_promo by brand, because "a promo is set up per brand anyway."
lessons.wrongWhy: Each of the nine brands has 9 to 11 entries in the promo lookup, so every sales row matches all of its brand's promos at once. Row count becomes 1,173,847 instead of 118,449, and revenue becomes ₽1,262,668,596 instead of ₽126,911,191 — exactly tenfold. No single row is "wrong" in this: the join did precisely what it was asked to do.
lessons.selfCheck: Count the paths from a fact table to a lookup. More than one — either delete the extra one, or leave it inactive and switch it on explicitly inside a measure.
